title: The Fan-Out Problem
description: Understand how social media feeds work at scale — fan-out on write vs read, the celebrity problem, timeline caching, and trending topics.

segments.text: You post a photo. Within seconds, it appears in the feeds of your five hundred followers. Simple, right? At Twitter's scale — five hundred million tweets per day — this is one of the hardest problems in distributed systems.

The naive approach: when a user opens their feed, query all the people they follow, fetch their recent posts, merge and sort by time. This is fan-out on read. It works, but it's slow — you're doing massive joins at read time.

The alternative: fan-out on write. When a user posts, immediately push that post into the pre-computed feed cache of every follower. Now when a user opens their feed, it's already assembled. Just read from cache. Lightning fast.

Fan-out on write trades storage and write amplification for fast reads. Each post is copied into hundreds or thousands of feed caches. You're spending resources at write time to make reads nearly free.
Now think about this. A celebrity like Taylor Swift has eighty million followers. She posts a tweet.
segments.thought_prompt: If we fan-out on write, we need to update 80 million feed caches for one tweet. Is that feasible?

segments.text: This is the celebrity problem. Fan-out on write for eighty million followers would take minutes and consume enormous resources. The solution? A hybrid approach. Regular users fan-out on write. Celebrities fan-out on read.

The timeline service merges these two sources. It reads the pre-computed feed cache for normal follows, then fetches and injects celebrity posts at read time. The merge is fast because celebrity posts are a tiny fraction of the total.

Each user's feed cache is a sorted list of post IDs stored in Redis, ordered by timestamp. We store only IDs, not full posts. When rendering the feed, a separate post service hydrates the IDs with content, images, and like counts.

Modern feeds aren't purely chronological. A ranking service scores posts by relevance — engagement signals, relationship closeness, content type. The timeline service applies this ranking before returning the feed.
Millions of tweets arrive every minute. How would you detect what's trending right now — topics spiking in the last few minutes compared to their baseline?
segments.thought_prompt: What data structures or algorithms would help detect trending topics in real-time?

segments.text: Trending detection uses stream processing. Count-min sketches approximate hashtag frequencies in constant space. Sliding windows compare the current rate to historical baselines. A topic is trending when its rate significantly exceeds its norm.

Designing a feed system is all about trade-offs. Fan-out on write for speed, fan-out on read for celebrities, a hybrid timeline service to merge them, and stream processing for trends. Every design decision is a trade-off at scale.
